newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel merger talks begin amid protests.
newsitem.headline: German steel merger talks begin amid protests.

text.p: The heads of Germany's biggest steel groups began talks on merging their steel operations on Thursday as workers and unions protested against a deal which they see as a mortal blow for Germany's "caring capitalism".

The talks are a bid to avert a hostile takeover launched this week by Fried. Krupp AG Krupp-Hoesch against its larger rival Thyssen AG which rocked the tradition of consensus among Germany's corporate, financial and political elite.

Thyssen chief executive Dieter Vogel and Krupp boss Gerhard Cromme met at a secret location to begin eight days of talks intended to merge their steel operations -- about one-third of turnover -- into a single unit. The merged firm would rank among Europe's top three steel producers.

Krupp has said if it cannot achieve an agreement, it will resurrect its takeover offer, which relies on banks to finance an offer which values Thyssen at 13.6 billion marks ($8.1 billion) and would create a steel giant with combined sales of 63 billion marks.

But the German daily Handelsblatt cited bankers advising the firms as saying Krupp remained determined to secure a full takeover of Thyssen, and saw a possible limited merger as only an intermediate step.

The bankers said Krupp had already secured control of 30 percent of Thyssen's shares held by friendly institutional investors, and had arranged a 15 billion mark credit line with banks, the paper said in advance release from Friday's edition. A Krupp spokesman declined to comment on the Handelsblatt report.
Analysts agree Germany's steel industry must rationalise.
But Krupp has shocked politicians and the public alike with what is seen as a cloak-and-dagger attack on a bigger company made vulnerable by the fact that its shares are widely strewn.

Workers at both Krupp and Thyssen began a third day of protest stoppages -- a tactic which has helped to mobilise public opinion against the deal seen as having been agreed in backrooms between Krupp and its bankers, led by Deutsche Bank.

Krupp's steel production operations were run down to emergency levels as workers marched to a meeting in Dortmund. Production at Thyssen's Duisburg works was also hit as 1,000 workers downed tools to join the meeting in solidarity.

The state of North Rhine-Westphalia, home to most of Germany's smokestack industry, reacted with horror at the prospect of more job losses for the depressed Ruhr Valley and persuaded Krupp and Thyssen to discuss a more limited merger.
State Economics Minister Wolfgang Clement told the state assembly that even the "alternative to the drastic course will not only secure jobs, but also cost jobs".

But state Finance Minister Heinz Schleusser told the Koelnische Rundschau daily he was "cautiously optimistic that the talks can lead to a result that will again emphasise cooperation between the two firms".
Shares in both companies were suspended on Tuesday and Wednesday but resumed bourse trading on Thursday.

Thyssen's shares closed at 375.80 marks compared with their March 17 after-hours close of 344.50, still well below Krupp's announced offer of 435 marks per share. Krupp stock closed at 313 marks against 270 marks on Monday, while the overall DAX index of leading German shares fell 1.55 percent.
Analysts agree that Krupp -- with 70,000 employees to Thyssen's 124,000 -- has a far stronger negotiating position.

With the support of Germany's two biggest banks, Deutsche and Dresdner, it can almost certainly force through a takeover if it wants to, despite a debt burden of three billion marks and the fact it says it does not yet control any Thyssen shares.
But public and employee sentiment remain important at a time when unemployment has soared to its highest level since 1933.

The mass-circulation daily Bild reflected a widespread feeling that Germany is abandoning a post-war tradition, based on consensus between companies, financiers, politicians and workers, which paid little attention to financial markets.

"If the banks encourage this return to primitive capitalism and our politicians put up with it, social peace and the future of this republic are in danger," its editorial said. ($ = 1.686 German Marks)
